targets.title: Impact of a mentoring and skills group program on mental health outcomes for maltreated children in foster care.
targets.evidence_quote: A pilot RCT with 156 youth found positive impacts on multi-informant (child, caregiver, teacher) reports of mental health functioning (including trauma symptoms), mental health services, and quality of life ( Taussig & Culhane, 2010 ). The current study sought to replicate and extend the mental health findings of the pilot FHF trial by adding data from five additional cohorts ( N =270) as well as examine moderating effects.
targets.outcome_quote: Intervention youth scored significantly lower on the mental health index ( β = −.11; t = −2.32; p < .05), posttraumatic stress symptoms ( β = −.09; t = −2.01; p < .05) and dissociation scales ( β = −.12; t = −2.76; p < .01), and they were less likely to be receiving mental health treatment at T2 (B = −.47; Wald = 4.43; p =.04). Intervention and control groups did not differ on quality of life or psychotropic medication use.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original pilot showed improvements in mental health, services and quality of life. This study confirms the first two but finds no quality-of-life difference. Discussion confirms particular benefits, without an overall replication verdict covering all outcomes.

targets.title: The moderating effect of risk exposure on an efficacious intervention for maltreated children.
targets.evidence_quote: In the FHF pilot study we found that (1) severity of neglect did not moderate outcomes, suggesting that children with severe neglect histories were just as likely to benefit from the intervention as those with less severe neglect histories ( Taussig, Culhane, Garrido, Knudtson, & Petrenko, 2013 ) but that (2) level of risk (i.e., exposure to ACEs) did moderate some outcomes (i.e., posttraumatic stress and dissociative symptoms), such that maltreated children exposed to a relatively higher number of ACEs did not experience the same reduction in trauma symptoms as children exposed to fewer adversities ( Weiler & Taussig, 2017 ). There were no a priori hypotheses about the direction of the potential moderating effects with the exception of the ACEs measure; based on our prior research, we hypothesized that those children with fewer ACEs would demonstrate greater program effects on trauma symptomatology.
targets.outcome_quote: Forty-two analyses were conducted and three interaction terms were statistically significant. The baseline ACEs measure significantly moderated the intervention’s impact on T2 youth-reported posttraumatic stress symptoms ( β = .15; t = 2.23; p < .05) and quality of life ( β = −.15; t = −2.06; p < .05).
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original risk moderation affected posttraumatic stress and dissociation; only posttraumatic stress moderation recurs among those two. Quality-of-life moderation is additional. Discussion confirms the fewer-ACEs pattern on some outcomes, rather than an overall verdict covering both original trauma outcomes. The new cohorts are pooled with the pilot sample, so the test is only partly independent.

reasoning: Title, DOI and six authors verified in complete author manuscript with references. New cohorts extend a published trial, with original pilot data pooled into the enlarged sample. Both intervention effects and the published ACE moderation finding are explicitly tested. Prior descriptions of the program, measure papers, and unrelated interventions are not targets.
